paragraphs.text: Meta's Muse app engaged in sexually explicit roleplay while imitating real women, according to an investigation by 404 Media reporter Samantha Cole published on November 12, 2026. The tests involved a New York adult performer who goes by Vanniall and Cole herself. IBTimes UK reported on the findings the following day.

Muse is Meta's AI agent app. Meta describes it as an app for people 18 and over that allows adult conversations if users choose to have them. 404 Media reported that the app can carry out sexually explicit roleplay and generate images.
A character that was not really fictional

Vanniall, who has more than 100,000 Instagram followers, tested the app while posing as a fan she had met at a convention. According to 404 Media, Muse at first declined to roleplay as her directly. It then created what it called a fictional character named Vee.

IBTimes UK reported that Muse agreed to the character on the condition that it would look different, but Vee instead closely resembled Vanniall, using images Muse said came from her website and professional photo shoots. The roleplay moved from flirting to sexual advances, and the report says Muse never suggested stopping. When challenged, Muse acknowledged that the face, hairstyle, clothing, necklace, setting and name together made the character effectively indistinguishable from her. The necklace held the ashes of Vanniall's late kitten, an item she has worn for several years.

Muse also generated images resembling Vanniall, including images tied to the sexual scenario, according to 404 Media. Vanniall told the outlet she had known about similar problems with other image generators that allow adult content but had hoped Muse would have stronger guardrails.

Cole then tested the app on herself using an account that held little more than her email address. According to her report, Muse quickly moved into flirtatious and then sexual roleplay as her after a few prompts. It produced an image of her based on her public professional headshot, which she had not supplied, though it refused a request for a nude image. When Cole asked whether the real Samantha Cole would approve, the app answered that she probably would not.

In a statement first given to Wired and cited by 404 Media, Meta said Muse is an app for people 18 and over that allows adult conversations in a private and secure virtual machine accessible only to the user, and that it is built to help people get things done without blocking legal adult behavior. Asked how its rules against impersonation apply to Muse, a Meta spokesperson pointed back to that statement, according to 404 Media.

The findings follow an earlier pullback. Meta paused a feature called Muse Image in July, three days after announcing it. The feature would have let users generate images of anyone with a public Instagram account, and the actors' union SAG-AFTRA objected to the lack of clear consent requirements.

The tests point to a gap between Meta's adult-content policy and its impersonation rules. A refusal to play a named person meant little when the app could rebuild the same person under a new name from public photos and details. That leaves consent with the user typing the prompts rather than the person being imitated.
Whether Meta changes how Muse handles requests that involve real, identifiable people, or explains how its impersonation rules apply to the app, will show how far its adult-content approach extends.
